title: Identity and transpose
objectives: Use the identity matrix and the transpose, including $(\mathbf{AB})^T = \mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T$.

screens.title: Four quarter turns
screens.prose: $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ turns the plane a quarter turn. Apply it four times in a row: $\mathbf{R}^4 = \mathbf{RRRR}$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{R}^4$.

hints.text: Follow $\mathbf{e}_1$ through four quarter turns.
$\mathbf{e}_1$ points up, then left, then down, then...
After four quarter turns every arrow is back where it started. So $\mathbf{e}_1 \to (1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 \to (0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: Four quarter turns make a full turn, so nothing has moved.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Column 1 is where $\mathbf{e}_1$ ends after four quarter turns.

byKey.r0c1: Column 1 is where $\mathbf{e}_1$ ends: back at $(1, 0)$.
byKey.r1c1: Column 1 is where $\mathbf{e}_1$ ends: back at $(1, 0)$.
byKey.r0c2: Column 2 is where $\mathbf{e}_2$ ends: back at $(0, 1)$.
byKey.r1c2: Column 2 is where $\mathbf{e}_2$ ends: back at $(0, 1)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{e}_1$ goes up, left, down and home again. $\mathbf{e}_2$ does the same, a quarter turn behind. So $\mathbf{R}^4 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: the matrix that moves nothing.

screens.title: The identity
screens.prose: A matrix that leaves every vector alone is an **identity**, $\mathbf{I}$. Its columns are $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots$ themselves, so $\mathbf{I}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}$. Then $\mathbf{AI} = \mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{IA} = \mathbf{A}$, whenever the sizes fit.
screens.question: Which identity makes $\mathbf{AI} = \mathbf{A}$ work?

options.why: In $\mathbf{AI}$, the rows of $\mathbf{I}$ must match the 3 columns of $\mathbf{A}$. The $2 \times 2$ one fits on the left: $\mathbf{IA}$.

options.text: There is only one identity matrix
options.why: There is one for each size. $\mathbf{AI}$ needs $3 \times 3$; $\mathbf{IA}$ needs $2 \times 2$.

hints.text: $(m \times n)(n \times p)$: the inner sizes must match.
$\mathbf{A}$ has 3 columns, so $\mathbf{I}$ on its right needs 3 rows.
An identity is square, so it is $3 \times 3$.

feedback.correct: $(2 \times 3)(3 \times 3)$ gives $2 \times 3$, and each column of $\mathbf{A}$ comes back unchanged.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the rows of $\mathbf{I}$ to the columns of $\mathbf{A}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{AI}$ multiplies $\mathbf{A}$ by each column of $\mathbf{I}$, which is some $\mathbf{e}_j$ with 3 entries. $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_j$ is column $j$ of $\mathbf{A}$, so $\mathbf{AI} = \mathbf{A}$. On the left, $\mathbf{IA} = \mathbf{A}$ needs the $2 \times 2$ identity.

screens.title: Flip the table
screens.prose: $\mathbf{D}$ holds daily returns in %. Rows are two days; columns are three stocks. We want the same numbers with one row per stock instead.

state.caption: Rows: Monday, Tuesday. Columns: stocks A, B and C.

screens.question: Tap the entries that become the first row of the flipped table.

hints.text: The first row of the new table belongs to stock A.
Stock A's returns run down column 1 of $\mathbf{D}$.
Tap 1.2 and $-0.6$: stock A on Monday and on Tuesday.

feedback.correct: Stock A's two returns, from column 1, become row 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find stock A's returns. They run down a column of $\mathbf{D}$.

byKey.row: You tapped Monday's returns: a row. Stock A's returns run down column 1.
byKey.D-0-1: That is stock B on Monday. Row 1 of the new table is stock A, column 1 of $\mathbf{D}$.
byKey.D-0-2: That is stock C on Monday. Row 1 of the new table is stock A, column 1 of $\mathbf{D}$.
byKey.D-1-1: That is stock B on Tuesday. Row 1 of the new table is stock A, column 1 of $\mathbf{D}$.
byKey.D-1-2: That is stock C on Tuesday. Row 1 of the new table is stock A, column 1 of $\mathbf{D}$.

explain.text: Column 1 of $\mathbf{D}$ becomes row 1. Swapping rows with columns is the **transpose**, $(\mathbf{D}^T)_{ij} = d_{ji}$. Here $\mathbf{D}^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1.2 & -0.6 \\ -0.4 & 0.3 \\ 0.8 & 1.1 \end{pmatrix}$, a $3 \times 2$ matrix.

screens.title: A row times a column
screens.prose: From now on a vector is a column: $\mathbf{u} = (3, 1)$ is $2 \times 1$. So its transpose $\mathbf{u}^T$ is a $1 \times 2$ row.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v}$ for $\mathbf{v} = (2, 4)$?

options.why: That is $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T$: a column times a row, which is $2 \times 2$. Here the row comes first.
You multiplied matching entries but did not add. A row times a column adds the products.

hints.text: $(1 \times 2)(2 \times 1)$ gives what size?
One row times one column is one dot product.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A $1 \times 2$ row times a $2 \times 1$ column is a single number.

explain.text: $\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v} = 3 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 4 = 10$, exactly the dot product. So $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v}$, and a $1 \times 1$ matrix is just a number.

hints.text: Entry $(1, 1)$ is row 1 of $\mathbf{B}^T$ dotted with column 1 of $\mathbf{A}^T$.
Row 1 of $\mathbf{B}^T$ is $(1, 3)$; column 1 of $\mathbf{A}^T$ is $(1, 2)$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T = \begin{pmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Keep it for the next screen.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each row of the first matrix with each column of the second.

explain.text: You got $\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Each entry is a row of $\mathbf{B}^T$ dotted with a column of $\mathbf{A}^T$.

screens.title: Keep the order?
screens.prose: Most people guess the transpose of a product keeps the order: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{B}^T$. Here it is for the same $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.
screens.question: Which product equals $(\mathbf{AB})^T$ for every $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$?

options.why: You transposed each factor and kept the order. The canvas shows $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{B}^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 7 \end{pmatrix}$, not $\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
Here $\mathbf{BA} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7 \end{pmatrix}$. Swapping the order alone is not enough; each factor is transposed too.
$\mathbf{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 7 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Its transpose swaps the 2 and the 3, so it is a different matrix.

hints.text: Compare the canvas with $(\mathbf{AB})^T$. Does the guess work?
On the last screen you computed $\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T$. Compare it with the caption.
$\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T$ gave $\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

feedback.correct: $(\mathbf{AB})^T = \mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T$: transpose each factor and reverse the order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each option against $(\mathbf{AB})^T = \begin{pmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

byKey.same: You transposed each factor and kept the order. That gives $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 7 \end{pmatrix}$ here, not $(\mathbf{AB})^T$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{B}^T$ came out as $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 7 \end{pmatrix}$, so the guess fails. Reversing the order, $\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T$, matched. The row of $\mathbf{A}$ and the column of $\mathbf{B}$ trade places, so the factors swap.

screens.title: Why the order reverses
screens.prose: The rule you found: $$(\mathbf{AB})^T = \mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T.$$ We check it one entry at a time, for entry $(i, j)$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $= (\text{row } j \text{ of } \mathbf{A}) \cdot (\text{column } i \text{ of } \mathbf{B})$: the product rule
$= (\text{column } i \text{ of } \mathbf{B}) \cdot (\text{row } j \text{ of } \mathbf{A})$: a dot product can be taken in either order
$= (\text{row } i \text{ of } \mathbf{B}^T) \cdot (\text{column } j \text{ of } \mathbf{A}^T)$: transposing turns columns into rows

hints.text: Start by undoing the outer transpose.
The swap of the two dot-product factors is the key step.
Swap indices, product rule, swap the dot product, rename rows and columns, product rule.

feedback.correct: The order reverses because the row of $\mathbf{A}$ and the column of $\mathbf{B}$ trade places.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the transpose of the product and end with the product of the transposes.

byKey.comm: Swapping the two vectors needs the dot product written out first.
byKey.done: The last line is the goal, so it comes at the end.

explain.text: Each line changes only how the same number is written. The key step swaps the two vectors in a dot product, which changes nothing. Read in the transposes, that swap is the reversed order.

screens.title: A symmetric matrix
screens.prose: A covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ holds $\mathrm{Cov}(R_i, R_j)$ in entry $(i, j)$. Two assets have variances 0.04 and 0.01, and $\mathrm{Cov}(R_1, R_2) = 0.006$.
screens.question: What is the hidden entry $(2, 1)$?

hints.text: Entry $(2, 1)$ is $\mathrm{Cov}(R_2, R_1)$.
Does the covariance of two returns depend on which you name first?
$\mathrm{Cov}(R_2, R_1)$ averages $(R_2 - \mu_2)(R_1 - \mu_1)$: the same product as for $\mathrm{Cov}(R_1, R_2)$, in the other order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Entry $(2, 1)$ is $\mathrm{Cov}(R_2, R_1)$. Compare it with entry $(1, 2)$.

byKey.corr: 0.3 would be a correlation. The matrix holds covariances, and entry $(1, 2)$ already gives 0.006.
byKey.neg: Swapping the order of two returns does not change the sign of their covariance.
byKey.zero: The two returns do move together: entry $(1, 2)$ is 0.006, and entry $(2, 1)$ is the same covariance.

explain.text: Covariance does not care about order, so entry $(2, 1)$ equals entry $(1, 2)$: 0.006. Then $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^T = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and we call $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ **symmetric**. Every covariance matrix is symmetric about its diagonal.

screens.title: Portfolio variance
screens.prose: Two assets have volatility 20% and 10% and correlation 0.3; their covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is below. You hold 60% and 40%: $\mathbf{w} = (0.6, 0.4)$. The portfolio's variance is $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$.
screens.question: Compute $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$.

hints.text: First find $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$, a column. Then dot $\mathbf{w}$ with it.
Top entry of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$: $0.024 + 0.0024 = 0.0264$. Bottom entry: $0.0036 + 0.004 = 0.0076$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$ first, then take $\mathbf{w}^T$ of it.

byKey.no-cross: You used only the diagonal: $0.36 \times 0.04 + 0.16 \times 0.01$. The covariance terms add $2 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.006$.
byKey.one-cross: You counted the covariance once. It sits in two entries, $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$, so it counts twice.
byKey.corr: You put the correlation 0.3 off the diagonal. $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ holds the covariance, $0.3 \times 0.2 \times 0.1 = 0.006$.

explain.text: The terms are $0.6^2 \times 0.04 = 0.0144$ and $0.4^2 \times 0.01 = 0.0016$, plus the covariance twice, once per off-diagonal entry: $2 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.006 = 0.00288$. They add to 0.01888. The volatility is $\sqrt{0.01888} \approx 0.1374$, about 13.74%, below the 16% weighted average of 20% and 10%.

ideas: The identity $\mathbf{I}$ has columns $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots$: it moves nothing, and $\mathbf{AI} = \mathbf{IA} = \mathbf{A}$ when the sizes fit.
The transpose swaps rows and columns: $(\mathbf{A}^T)_{ij} = a_{ji}$. A dot product is $\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v}$.
A covariance matrix is symmetric, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^T = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and a portfolio's variance is $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$.

formula.name: Transpose of a product
formula.note: Transpose each factor and reverse the order.

options.why: Transposing swaps rows and columns, so the sizes swap too.
A transpose has the same entries rearranged: 6 of them, not 9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each column of $\mathbf{A}$ becomes a row of $\mathbf{A}^T$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}$ has 3 columns, each with 2 entries. They become 3 rows of 2 entries: $3 \times 2$.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are square matrices of the same size.
quiz.question: What is $(\mathbf{ABC})^T$?

options.why: You kept the order. Transposing a product reverses it.
You moved only $\mathbf{C}$. Apply the rule twice: $(\mathbf{AB})\mathbf{C}$ gives $\mathbf{C}^T(\mathbf{AB})^T$, and then $(\mathbf{AB})^T = \mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat $\mathbf{ABC}$ as $(\mathbf{AB})\mathbf{C}$ and use the rule twice.

explain.text: Write $\mathbf{ABC}$ as $(\mathbf{AB})\mathbf{C}$. The rule gives $\mathbf{C}^T(\mathbf{AB})^T$, and using it again gives $\mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T$.

quiz.question: What is its volatility, the standard deviation?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Volatility is the square root of the variance.

byKey.no-root: That is the variance as a percentage. Take the square root first.
byKey.average: That is the weighted average of 20% and 10%. With correlation 0.3, the mix is less volatile than that.

explain.text: Volatility is $\sqrt{0.01888} \approx 0.1374$, or 13.74%. It is below the 16% average because the two assets are not perfectly correlated.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ is any matrix, square or not.
quiz.question: Which of these is always symmetric?

options.why: $\mathbf{A}^2$ needs $\mathbf{A}$ square, and even then it can fail: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric.
Adding $\mathbf{I}$ changes only the diagonal. If $\mathbf{A}$ is not symmetric, neither is $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}$.
$\mathbf{A}^T$ is symmetric only when $\mathbf{A}$ is. For $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ it is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Transpose each option with the reversal rule and see which comes back unchanged.

explain.text: Use the reversal rule: $(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^T = \mathbf{A}^T(\mathbf{A}^T)^T = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$. It equals its own transpose for every $\mathbf{A}$. Covariance matrices are built this way from centred data.
